title: Data Structures for Backend Engineers
goal: Choose structures by the operations and constraints of the problem.

topics.title: Big-O
topics.description: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size, not exact elapsed time.
learningGoals: Time and space costs name their input size
Worst and average behavior are distinguished
examples: Search a list of n sessions for an ID.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size, not exact elapsed time. State the operation and assumptions before quoting complexity. Distinguish average, worst-case, and amortized behavior, and consider memory as well as time.

workedExample.scenario: Search a list of n sessions for an ID.
steps: A missing ID can inspect all n entries.
Doubling n can double comparisons.

commonMistakes: O(1) does not mean zero cost or always faster for tiny inputs.
material.independentExercise: Analyze a deduplication algorithm with and without a set.
recallQuestions: What is n in your analysis?
Which assumptions support the claimed complexity?

acceptanceCriteria: Time and space costs name their input size
Worst and average behavior are distinguished

topics.title: Array
topics.description: An array holds a fixed number of positions with indexed access.
learningGoals: Index boundaries are tested
Returned storage cannot mutate protected state
examples: Store three counters in an array.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: An array holds a fixed number of positions with indexed access. Growing requires another allocation and copying. Arrays of references do not make their objects immutable, and invalid indexes must be considered at boundaries.

workedExample.scenario: Store three counters in an array.
steps: Read index two directly.
Index three is outside the valid range.

commonMistakes: A final array reference does not freeze its elements.
guidedExercise: Copy an array before exposing it
material.independentExercise: Model fixed hourly buckets and explain rollover behavior.
recallQuestions: When must an array be copied?
What is fixed about its size?

acceptanceCriteria: Index boundaries are tested
Returned storage cannot mutate protected state

topics.title: ArrayList
topics.description: ArrayList offers indexed access over a growable array.
learningGoals: Operation costs are correctly explained
Order remains correct after mutation

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: ArrayList offers indexed access over a growable array. Appends are amortized constant time, but a resize copies elements and insertion or removal near the front shifts later values. Use it for ordinary sequences unless requirements suggest otherwise.

steps: Remove the first.
Later elements shift to earlier positions.

commonMistakes: Amortized O(1) does not mean every append costs the same.
material.independentExercise: Store audit events and explain why it is unsuitable as a large front-removal queue.
recallQuestions: Why is append amortized?
Which operations require shifting?

acceptanceCriteria: Operation costs are correctly explained
Order remains correct after mutation

topics.title: LinkedList
topics.description: Linked lists connect nodes rather than storing a contiguous sequence.
learningGoals: Search cost is included in analysis
A collection choice follows actual operations
examples: Read the middle of a long LinkedList.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Linked lists connect nodes rather than storing a contiguous sequence. Locating an indexed element still requires traversal. Constant-time unlinking only helps once the relevant position is already available; extra allocations and locality also matter.

workedExample.scenario: Read the middle of a long LinkedList.
steps: Traverse nodes to reach it.
Removing by index includes that search cost.

commonMistakes: LinkedList is not automatically faster for every insertion or removal.
material.independentExercise: Explain when an ArrayList or ArrayDeque better matches backend work.
recallQuestions: What must be found before unlinking?
Why can asymptotic equality hide practical costs?

acceptanceCriteria: Search cost is included in analysis
A collection choice follows actual operations

topics.title: Stack
topics.description: A stack returns the most recently added value first.
learningGoals: Pop order is LIFO
Unbalanced and empty cases have explicit outcomes

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A stack returns the most recently added value first. It supports nested traversal and undo-like work. In Java, Deque implementations can provide stack operations; learn the behavior rather than depending on the legacy Stack class.

steps: Pop returns B.
The next pop returns A.

commonMistakes: FIFO and LIFO are different contracts even when methods look similar.
material.independentExercise: Use a stack to validate simple balanced delimiters.
recallQuestions: Which item leaves first?
When is empty input a valid result?

acceptanceCriteria: Pop order is LIFO
Unbalanced and empty cases have explicit outcomes

topics.title: Queue
topics.description: A queue generally models first-in-first-out processing.
learningGoals: FIFO behavior is tested
Failure and capacity policies are explicit

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A queue generally models first-in-first-out processing. Separate adding, retrieving, and empty behavior. A real job queue also needs capacity and failure policies; collection order alone does not guarantee reliable delivery.

steps: Poll EMAIL first.
A failure policy decides whether it retries or moves elsewhere.

commonMistakes: Removing a job before handling failure can lose work.
guidedExercise: Define behavior when empty or full
material.independentExercise: Write a single-process queue with a documented retry and capacity policy.
recallQuestions: What happens after processing fails?
What limits queued memory?

acceptanceCriteria: FIFO behavior is tested
Failure and capacity policies are explicit

topics.title: Deque
topics.description: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends.
learningGoals: End choices match the declared order
Empty and capacity cases are covered
examples: Add A and B at the tail.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends. It can implement FIFO or LIFO depending on which ends you use. Choose method names that make the intended order obvious and document empty-operation behavior.

workedExample.scenario: Add A and B at the tail.
steps: Remove from the head for FIFO.
Remove from the tail for LIFO.

commonMistakes: Mixing ends accidentally can change the processing contract.
guidedExercise: Compare queue and stack operations on ArrayDeque
material.independentExercise: Implement a bounded recent-event buffer that drops the oldest value.
recallQuestions: Which ends implement FIFO?
Why might polling differ from removing?

acceptanceCriteria: End choices match the declared order
Empty and capacity cases are covered

topics.title: HashMap
topics.description: HashMap uses hashes to find candidate keys and equality to identify a match.
learningGoals: Custom keys obey equals/hashCode
Collision and missing-key cases work
examples: Two session keys share a hash.

tasks.title: Explain HashMap in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: HashMap uses hashes to find candidate keys and equality to identify a match. Average lookup is constant time under suitable conditions, not a universal worst-case promise. Ordinary HashMap does not provide atomic multi-threaded workflows.

workedExample.scenario: Two session keys share a hash.
steps: Equality distinguishes them.
Both stored sessions remain retrievable.

commonMistakes: A hash collision is not a duplicate key.
material.independentExercise: Index sessions by a stable ID and compare lookup with a scan.
recallQuestions: What distinguishes colliding keys?
Which concurrency guarantee is absent?

acceptanceCriteria: Custom keys obey equals/hashCode
Collision and missing-key cases work

topics.title: HashSet
topics.description: HashSet uses hash-based membership to detect repeated values.
learningGoals: Duplicates within the horizon are detected
Memory-retention limitations are stated

tasks.title: Explain HashSet in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: HashSet uses hash-based membership to detect repeated values. Memory grows with retained entries, so decide how long request IDs must remain. It is not a complete durable or cross-instance idempotency solution.

steps: Only the first insertion is new.
Expired IDs can be removed according to policy.

commonMistakes: Keeping every ID forever makes a simple detector unbounded.
material.independentExercise: Build a request detector with a clock and predictable cleanup.
recallQuestions: What makes an ID safe to remove?
What happens across two process instances?

acceptanceCriteria: Duplicates within the horizon are detected
Memory-retention limitations are stated

topics.title: Tree
topics.description: Trees represent hierarchical relationships without cycles.
learningGoals: Traversal visits expected nodes
Parent and cycle rules are explicit

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Trees represent hierarchical relationships without cycles. Define roots, parent rules, and traversal order before implementation. For this track, understanding traversal and modeling is core; implementing a balanced tree is optional depth.

steps: Visit the department before its children.
Reject attaching an ancestor below its descendant.

commonMistakes: A hierarchy can become a graph if multiple parents are permitted.
material.independentExercise: List descendants while detecting malformed cycles.
recallQuestions: What makes a structure a tree?
When does traversal need cycle protection?

acceptanceCriteria: Traversal visits expected nodes
Parent and cycle rules are explicit

topics.title: Heap
topics.description: A heap maintains enough ordering to retrieve an extremum efficiently.
learningGoals: Minimum access follows the heap property
Sorted iteration is not assumed

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A heap maintains enough ordering to retrieve an extremum efficiently. It does not keep every element globally sorted. Learn how insert and remove restore the heap property before choosing it for scheduling.

steps: The minimum is 4.
Remaining internal order need not be sorted.

commonMistakes: Iterating a heap does not guarantee sorted output.
guidedExercise: Trace insertion into a small min-heap
Compare with sorting on every insertion
material.independentExercise: Explain a scheduler's insertion and earliest-removal costs.
recallQuestions: What property does a min-heap guarantee?
What ordering does it not guarantee?

acceptanceCriteria: Minimum access follows the heap property
Sorted iteration is not assumed

topics.title: PriorityQueue
topics.description: PriorityQueue exposes priority-based retrieval, typically backed by a heap.
learningGoals: Polling follows the comparator
Ties and empty queues are tested
examples: Jobs B and A share executeAt.

tasks.title: Explain PriorityQueue in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: PriorityQueue exposes priority-based retrieval, typically backed by a heap. The comparator determines which value wins; equal priorities need an explicit policy if deterministic ordering matters. It is not a FIFO queue or a thread-safe scheduler.

workedExample.scenario: Jobs B and A share executeAt.
steps: Compare sequence numbers after time.
The earlier sequence wins the tie.

commonMistakes: Queue iteration is not the same as polling in priority order.
material.independentExercise: Schedule jobs with equal deadlines and document synchronization ownership.
recallQuestions: How are ties resolved?
What differs between iteration and polling?

acceptanceCriteria: Polling follows the comparator
Ties and empty queues are tested

topics.title: Graph basics
topics.description: Graphs model relationships such as prerequisites.
learningGoals: Every prerequisite precedes its dependent
Cycles are reported explicitly
examples: B depends on A and C depends on B.

tasks.title: Explain Graph basics in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Graphs model relationships such as prerequisites. Define edge direction explicitly and track visited nodes during traversal. A dependency cycle prevents a valid topological ordering and should be reported rather than recursed through indefinitely.

workedExample.scenario: B depends on A and C depends on B.
steps: A can be learned before B.
Adding A depends on C creates a cycle.

commonMistakes: A visited set and a current recursion path serve different purposes.
material.independentExercise: Order a small dependency graph with disconnected nodes.
recallQuestions: Which direction does an edge represent?
Why can a cycle block scheduling?

acceptanceCriteria: Every prerequisite precedes its dependent
Cycles are reported explicitly

topics.title: Sorting
topics.description: Sorting imposes an order using a comparison rule.
learningGoals: Extreme and equal values sort correctly
Input mutation policy is documented
examples: Sort jobs by time then ID.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Sorting imposes an order using a comparison rule. A comparator must be consistent and avoid overflow-prone arithmetic subtraction. Decide whether equal elements must retain original order and whether mutation of the input is acceptable.

workedExample.scenario: Sort jobs by time then ID.
steps: Compare fields explicitly.
Test equal times and extreme values.

commonMistakes: Returning a-b can overflow and reverse the intended comparison.
material.independentExercise: Order audit records without mutating the caller's input.
recallQuestions: What makes a comparator consistent?
When does stability matter?

acceptanceCriteria: Extreme and equal values sort correctly
Input mutation policy is documented

topics.title: Binary search
topics.description: Binary search repeatedly halves an ordered search range.
learningGoals: Empty, missing, and duplicate cases pass
Each iteration shrinks the range

tasks.title: Explain Binary search in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves an ordered search range. Correctness depends on sorting and consistent bounds. Define whether you want an exact match, first match, or insertion point; duplicates make those different problems.

steps: Keep the left candidate after a match.
Finish at index one.

commonMistakes: Finding some matching element does not find the first duplicate.
material.independentExercise: Find the first job at or after a requested time.
recallQuestions: Why must the input be ordered?
How do duplicate requirements change the algorithm?

acceptanceCriteria: Empty, missing, and duplicate cases pass
Each iteration shrinks the range

topics.title: Thread safety and atomic operations

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Thread-safe individual methods do not automatically make a multi-step operation atomic.
learningGoals: The stated cap survives competing calls
Cross-instance limitations are explicit

material.explanation: Thread-safe individual methods do not automatically make a multi-step operation atomic. Identify the state transition that must have one winner. A local lock can protect one process, but it cannot coordinate separate application instances.

steps: A protected check-and-increment admits only one.
A separate check followed by increment can admit both.

commonMistakes: Concurrent collections do not fix every compound workflow.
guidedExercise: Protect the full transition with a single lock
material.independentExercise: Test the rate limiter with competing callers and document its process-local scope.
recallQuestions: Which steps must be atomic together?
What can a JVM lock not coordinate?

acceptanceCriteria: The stated cap survives competing calls
Cross-instance limitations are explicit

examples: R1 arrives twice within the horizon.

Explain lookup complexity
Measure memory usage
Consider millions of entries
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Repeated IDs inside the horizon are detected
Verify: Retention is testable and memory policy is explicit

requirements: Use a HashSet for request IDs in a single-process exercise
A repeated ID is detected within a declared retention horizon
Use a Clock for expiration or define a deliberate fixed-capacity policy
State average lookup and memory growth
Describe what changes with millions of entries or multiple instances

deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: Membership solves one part of deduplication. Retention determines memory use and how long duplicate protection lasts. Record the correctness tradeoff if you evict IDs early or limit capacity; a rejected or retried business effect needs a larger contract.

workedExample.scenario: R1 arrives twice within the horizon.
steps: The second is detected.
After policy expiration, R1 may be admitted again under the stated contract.

Retention is testable and memory policy is explicit
Restart and cross-instance limitations are documented

Process FIFO
Define behavior for failed jobs
Check boundary and failure cases

Verify: Capacity cannot grow without bound

material.explanation: Separate the ordering contract from delivery reliability. A collection can establish FIFO retrieval, but processing failures and process restarts require deliberate policies. Keep the first implementation small and document where its guarantees stop.

steps: EMAIL is processed first.

The 12:05 job stays pending.

challenges.title: In-memory Rate Limiter
challenges.description: Implement a precisely defined process-local rate limit with a clock and concurrency check.
learningGoals: Implement a precisely defined process-local rate limit with a clock and concurrency check.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.

tasks.title: Requirements and window rules
Data structure choice
Algorithm
Boundary and concurrency tests
Verify: Exactly 100 requests can be admitted per user and fixed bucket
Verify: The 101st rejects and a different user retains its own allowance
Verify: Boundary behavior is deterministic without sleeping tests
Verify: Competing local callers cannot exceed the bucket cap
Verify: Stale-state cleanup and process-local limits are documented

requirements: Allow at most 100 requests per user per fixed UTC-minute bucket
Buckets start at multiples of 60 seconds; explain why adjacent buckets permit bursts
The 101st request in the same bucket is rejected without increasing admitted count
A new bucket resets that user allowance; users are independent
Make the full check-and-increment atomic for competing local threads
Remove stale user entries and describe cleanup work and memory limits
Document restart behavior and lack of cross-instance enforcement
constraints: In-memory only; no Redis or database
Use standard collections and a controllable time source
A simple lock is acceptable if its throughput ceiling is documented

material.explanation: Choose one window model and make it executable. Fixed windows are intentionally simple but do not promise at most 100 across every rolling 60-second span. Synchronization must protect the compound decision, while cleanup prevents permanently retaining inactive users.

steps: The 101st in that bucket rejects.
At 12:01Z a new bucket admits U1 under the fixed-window rule.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Test requests 1, 100, and 101 for one user.
Use fixed times before and at a boundary.
Coordinate competing callers with a barrier rather than a sleep.
material.independentExercise: Explain how a sliding-window contract would change state and memory costs without implementing it unless needed.
recallQuestions: Which burst can a fixed window allow?
What does the local lock fail to coordinate?

acceptanceCriteria: Exactly 100 requests can be admitted per user and fixed bucket
The 101st rejects and a different user retains its own allowance
Boundary behavior is deterministic without sleeping tests
Competing local callers cannot exceed the bucket cap
Stale-state cleanup and process-local limits are documented
